title: RESTAURA project: Using public participation GIS to explore technological risk, landscape, and health perceptions in Camp de Tarragona
author: Gheitasi, Albert, et al.
materials: Furthermore, a correlation matrix was generated to examine the relationship between the different types of risk-related variables (technological risk perception, landscape perception, and health perception). Both Pearson's correlation coefficient and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient are applied. These analyses were performed using Jamovi 2.6.17 statistical software.

steps.title: Conduct scoping review
steps.instruction: Perform a scoping review following the PRISMA‑SCR protocol to identify common approaches and survey questions used in participatory processes for assessing technological risk perception.

steps.title: Develop PPGIS survey platform
steps.instruction: Create the PPGIS questionnaire and implement the online platform, adapting the interface to Spanish and Catalan and enabling both single‑option and multiple‑option mapping.

steps.title: Distribute questionnaire
steps.instruction: Launch the survey through social‑media posts, e‑mail invitations, and QR‑code posters to maximise participation across the Camp de Tarragona case study.

steps.title: Clean spatial responses
steps.instruction: In ArcGIS Pro 3.3.0, use the Clip tool to remove all survey points located outside the Camp de Tarragona boundaries, correcting or discarding inaccurate records and reorganising the dataset for analysis.

steps.title: Run kernel density analysis
steps.instruction: Using ArcGIS Pro 3.3.0, perform kernel density analysis on the cleaned point layers (participants’ residences, perceived risk sources, and affected areas) to visualise spatial intensity of perceptions.

steps.title: Conduct distance analysis to green areas
steps.instruction: Apply the Near tool in ArcGIS Pro 3.3.0 to calculate the distance from each risk‑source point to the nearest green‑space polygon, producing a distance layer for further interpretation.

steps.title: Prepare InVEST urban nature model
steps.instruction: In InVEST 3.14.3, load a land‑use/land‑cover (LULC) raster with integer codes, a gridded population raster, and set the minimum urban‑nature requirement to 9 m² per capita; run the Urban Nature Access model and reclassify the continuous output raster into five quantile‑based categories (very low, low, medium, high, very high).

steps.title: Extract raster values to points
steps.instruction: Import the reclassified urban‑nature raster into ArcGIS Pro 3.3.0 and use the Extract Multi‑Value to Points tool to assign an access value to each survey point, creating an attribute table with this new field.

steps.title: Join spatial and survey attributes
steps.instruction: Join the point layer containing urban‑nature access values with the original PPGIS survey table (risk level, age, income, education) so each record holds both spatial and non‑spatial attributes.

steps.title: Clean non‑spatial survey data
steps.instruction: Review all questionnaire responses, discard any records outside the study boundaries, and organise the remaining data into three sections: socio‑demographic, picture‑based (landscape), and health‑related questions.

steps.title: Analyze socio‑demographic data
steps.instruction: Calculate percentages for each socio‑demographic category (age, education, income, gender) in Microsoft Excel; perform descriptive statistics in Excel and further exploratory analyses in Jamovi 2.6.17.

steps.title: Analyze picture‑based questionnaire
steps.instruction: For each original and manipulated photograph, compute the proportion of respondents selecting each emotion on the three bipolar scales (Anxious/Serene, Restless/Tranquil, Tense/Calm) using Excel; conduct statistical testing of these proportions in Jamovi 2.6.17.

steps.title: Score perceived stress scale
steps.instruction: Assign scores to the four PSS‑4 items (items 1 & 4: 0‑4; items 2 & 3 reverse‑coded 4‑0), sum the four scores to obtain a total stress score, and categorize the result as Low (0‑4), Medium (5‑8), High (9‑12) or Very High (13‑16) stress.

steps.title: Generate correlation matrix
steps.instruction: Using Jamovi 2.6.17, compute Pearson’s and Spearman’s correlation coefficients among technological risk perception, landscape perception, and health perception variables, and display the resulting matrix.

steps.title: Validate methodology in Tehran case
steps.instruction: Apply the full PPGIS workflow to the Tehran Oil Refinery study: deploy the survey in Farsi online and in‑person, collect 220 valid responses, clean the data, and obtain 741 georeferenced risk‑source points and 800 affected‑area points for analysis.

description: The proposed PPGIS methodology was first applied in the Tehran Oil Refinery case study to assess its operational feasibility, data quality, and analytical compatibility. The survey was successfully deployed in Farsi using a multi-page online interface and complemented by in-person data collection to ensure inclusivity. A total of 220 valid responses were collected. Participants identified 741 georeferenced points representing perceived technological risk sources and 800 points representing areas affected by technological risks after data cleaning. The spatial distribution of mapped risk sources showed a clear concentration in the southern part of Tehran, particularly within and around the oil refinery and its associated facilities, demonstrating the method's ability to capture spatially explicit perceptions aligned with known industrial infrastructures. The dataset allowed the integration of spatial information with socio-demographic and health-related variables. Stress levels, as calculated using the PSS-Studies, were successfully categorized, with the majority of respondents falling within the medium stress range. The collected data were compatible with kernel density analysis and statistical processing, confirming that the method generates structured and analyzable spatial and non-spatial outputs suitable for participatory risk perception studies. The detailed results and data collected in this study are available in the URV repository.5
